newsitem.title: USA: U.S CREDIT OUTLOOK - Lower tier data takes back seat.
newsitem.headline: U.S CREDIT OUTLOOK - Lower tier data takes back seat.

text.p: An economic calendar of lower tier data on Friday is expected to curtail activity in the U.S. Treasury market as traders look to next week's more significant economic numbers, U.S. economists said.

"There's not going to be a lot of enthusiasm over tomorrow's numbers," said Kim Rupert, economist at MMS International Inc. "We're in a fairly slow, consolidated mode going into the holiday (Thanksgiving Day) next week."
U.S. import and export prices for October are due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT. In September, import prices rose 0.8 percent while export prices dropped 0.8 percent.
Also due on Friday at 1400 EST/1900 GMT are U.S. federal budget figures for October. Economists expect the budget to have narrowed to $32 billion from September's $35.37 billion.

"We're at pretty high levels and buyers are kind of hesitant right here," Rupert added. "But then (they have) also gotten absolutely no satisfaction from trying to short the market, so I think we're kind of caught for the moment."

Said William Griggs, managing director at Griggs & Santow Inc: "We really don't have much coming tomorrow, but I think the (Treasury) market's in an optimistic mood. I don't see anything that's going to change that mood much."
"The only problem is it has run as far as you can imagine it running in the absence of something to help it along and I don't think we're going to get that tomorrow," Griggs added.
Next week's U.S. economic data include a revision to third quarter Gross Domestic Product and October durable goods.
Economists said the market's optimistic view, particularly in the front end, leaves limited potential for continued improvement. But some saw space for the longer end.
"You can always argue there's a little room in the long end...but the issue here is that the market has run so far it's going to be extremely difficult," Griggs added.
With the lack of more significant data until next week, economists noted that it has been unexpected elements that have pushed down yields in the market.
"The striking thing is that, while the data coming out next week do not look like the kinds of things that could move the market, the reality is these are the types of things that have," Griggs said.

Weakness in recent economic releases, such as October U.S. housing starts, existing home sales, weekly retail sales reports and the Chicago Purchasing Managment Index (PMI) have caused reaction in the marketplace, Griggs noted.

"Chicago PMI has been more important than NAPM (National Association of Purchasing Managers Index) in recent months," Griggs added. "The only thing that can change this market is any commentary coming out of the Fed (Federal Reserve), like we've begun seeing recently...(such as) that the market's ahead of itself," Griggs added.
"The market is assuming the next Fed move is an ease and that may not be the case...it wouldn't surprise me to see the Fed put that into better perspective in public talks," he added.
